title: Spectrophotometer Parts: Lamps, Cuvettes, PMT and Wavelength Checks
summary: Follow light through a spectrophotometer, match the lamp and cuvette material to UV or visible work, see how a photomultiplier amplifies the signal, and learn why holmium oxide (not didymium) checks the wavelength scale.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 4 High-Yield Hits 2 (light path), 3 (light sources), 5 (cuvettes), 6 (PMT) and 21 (wavelength QA checks), Exam Trap 2 (glass cuvette at 280 nm) and the chapter figure (light path; the app drawing is original). Checked against Khan 2019, Zacharioudaki 2022, Baral 2026, El Hosry 2023, González-Morales 2020, Whitehead 2017, Zheng 2020, Michail 2024, Reule 1976 and Allen 2007. Qualifications: Reule judged didymium glass unsuitable for wavelength checking (bands too wide, temperature-dependent, variable rare-earth content) and holmium oxide checks wavelength only (Allen); the reviewer’s ~90 V per dynode differs from the 100–200 V given in Michail 2024 (which gives overall gain of the order of 10⁶), and Zheng 2020 says “more than a million times”, so 10⁶ is not a ceiling; the sources read show glass absorbing UV-B/UV-C (below about 315 nm) rather than giving the reviewer’s 350 nm cut-off. Not taught as fact: the 350 nm and 2000 nm glass limits, deuterium ~100 V, the ~90 V dynode figure, the didymium ~600 nm peak, interference-filter bandwidths (Hit 4).

objectives: Put the parts of a spectrophotometer light path in order.
Match deuterium, tungsten-halogen, xenon and hollow cathode lamps, and glass or quartz cuvettes, to the wavelength region or method.
Explain how a photomultiplier tube amplifies a signal and how holmium oxide is used to check the wavelength scale.

scenes.title: A UV assay that sees nothing
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a new bench analyst sets up a protein assay read at 280 nm. She uses a silicate glass cuvette from the colorimetry drawer, and the instrument reports almost no usable light reaching the detector. Yesterday’s wavelength check was done with a didymium glass filter. Question token: “Which part of the light path failed?”

cues.text: Invented scenario: a new analyst sets up a protein assay read at two hundred and eighty nanometres, in the ultraviolet.
She grabs a glass cuvette from the colorimetry drawer, and almost no light reaches the detector. Yesterday’s wavelength check used a didymium glass filter.
Which part of the light path failed, and was that wavelength check good enough?

props.label: Which part of the light path failed?

scenes.title: The light path, in order
scenes.altText: Schematic light path drawn left to right as five boxes: light source → wavelength selector (monochromator with a prism or diffraction grating, plus slits) → cuvette holding the sample → photodetector → signal processing and readout. A note card below: the detector signal is compared with a reference (blank) to give transmittance and absorbance.

cues.text: A typical absorbance spectrophotometer follows this path. First, a light source makes the light.
Next, a wavelength selector, a monochromator with a prism or, more often, a diffraction grating, passes only the chosen wavelength through its exit slit.
That narrow band passes through the cuvette holding the sample, and a photodetector measures how much light gets through.
Finally, the electronics compare the sample signal with a blank or reference and report transmittance or absorbance.

props.label: Sample signal vs blank → transmittance → absorbance

scenes.title: Pick the lamp, pick the cuvette
scenes.altText: Lamp card: deuterium lamp = continuum in the ultraviolet (one review: about 160–400 nm); tungsten-halogen lamp = visible region, weak below 400 nm; xenon lamps = broad emission from the UV into the visible and beyond; hollow cathode lamp (atomic absorption) = cathode plated with the analyte metal, so it emits that element’s own lines. Cuvette card: glass transmits near-UV (UV-A) but absorbs UV-B and UV-C, while quartz (fused silica) transmits them, so deep-UV work needs quartz; the standard cuvette has a 10 mm (1 cm) path; within the Beer’s law range, absorbance is proportional to path length, so ten times the path gives ten times the absorbance.

cues.text: Choose the lamp by wavelength. A deuterium lamp gives a continuous spectrum in the ultraviolet. A tungsten-halogen lamp covers the visible region but is weak below four hundred nanometres, so a UV-visible instrument may carry both lamps.

Xenon lamps emit broadly from the ultraviolet into the visible. Atomic absorption is different: the cathode of its hollow cathode lamp is plated with the metal being measured, so it emits that element’s own lines.

Choose the cuvette by wavelength too. Glass passes the near ultraviolet but absorbs shorter ultraviolet light, while quartz, also called fused silica, lets it through. A reading at two hundred and eighty nanometres needs quartz.
The standard cuvette has a one-centimetre path. Within the range where Beer’s law holds, absorbance is proportional to path length, so a ten-centimetre path gives ten times the absorbance.

scenes.title: Detector and wavelength check
scenes.altText: Detector card: photomultiplier tube (PMT) — photon hits the photocathode → photoelectron is accelerated to the first dynode → each dynode releases more secondary electrons → anode collects the cascade; amplification of the order of a million-fold or more; gain depends on the voltage between dynodes (one review gives 100–200 V). Wavelength-check card: holmium oxide glass has sharp, certified bands (NIST lists 11, from about 241 to 638 nm, including 360.8 nm); didymium glass bands are too wide, temperature-dependent and vary in composition, so one older standards paper judged it unsuitable for wavelength checking; holmium checks the wavelength scale only, while neutral-density filters check the absorbance scale. Hook answer card: glass absorbed the 280 nm light (use quartz); recheck wavelength with holmium oxide.

cues.text: Many precision instruments use a photomultiplier tube. A photon frees an electron from the photocathode, and that electron is accelerated into a chain of dynodes. Each dynode releases more electrons, so the signal grows about a million-fold or more.
The gain depends on the voltage across the dynodes. One review gives one hundred to two hundred volts per step. Some instruments use photodiodes instead.

Check the wavelength scale with holmium oxide glass: its absorption bands are sharp, with certified positions such as three hundred sixty point eight nanometres. Didymium bands are broad and temperature-sensitive. Holmium checks wavelength only; neutral-density filters check the absorbance scale.
Back to the hook. The glass cuvette absorbed the ultraviolet light, so switch to quartz, and recheck the wavelength with holmium oxide.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A silicate glass cuvette works fine at 280 nm” (✓ glass absorbs short-wavelength UV; use quartz or fused silica); “A deuterium lamp is the light source for visible colorimetry” (✓ deuterium serves the UV; tungsten-halogen serves the visible); “A holmium oxide filter checks absorbance accuracy” (✓ holmium checks wavelength positions; neutral-density filters check the absorbance scale).

cues.text: Trap one: a glass cuvette works fine at two hundred and eighty nanometres. No: glass absorbs that ultraviolet light. Use quartz or fused silica.
Trap two: the deuterium lamp lights visible colorimetry. No: deuterium serves the ultraviolet, tungsten-halogen serves the visible.
Trap three: a holmium oxide filter checks absorbance accuracy. No: it checks wavelength positions. Neutral-density filters check the absorbance scale.

props.title: ✗ “Glass is fine at 280 nm.”
lines: ✓ Glass absorbs deep UV: use quartz

scenes.title: Deep, Tint, Quartz, Where
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “D for Deep UV, T for Tint: Deuterium lights the ultraviolet, Tungsten lights the colours. Quartz lets UV through. Holmium tells you WHERE you are on the wavelength scale, not HOW MUCH light was absorbed.” Tokens: D = deep UV · T = tint (visible) · Q = UV window · Ho = where. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: D for deep ultraviolet, T for tint. Deuterium lights the ultraviolet, tungsten lights the colours. Quartz lets ultraviolet through. Holmium tells you where you are on the wavelength scale, not how much light was absorbed.
Where it breaks: xenon lamps cover both regions; the exact wavelength where glass stops transmitting depends on the glass; and some instruments use photodiodes, not a photomultiplier.

lines: Glass cut-off depends on the glass

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Source → selector → cuvette → detector → readout”, “Deuterium + quartz for UV · tungsten-halogen + glass for visible · holmium checks wavelength”.

cues.text: Light runs from source to wavelength selector to cuvette to detector, so match a deuterium lamp and quartz cuvette to ultraviolet work, a tungsten-halogen lamp to visible work, and check the wavelength scale with holmium oxide.

props.label: UV: deuterium + quartz · visible: tungsten-halogen · holmium = wavelength

explanation.what: Plain language: a spectrophotometer makes light, picks one colour, shines it through the sample and measures what comes out. Each part must suit the wavelength: the lamp must emit it, the cuvette must let it through, and the wavelength dial must be checked against a standard with known sharp bands. Scientific terms: light source, monochromator (prism or diffraction grating, slits), cuvette (glass, quartz/fused silica), path length, photodetector, photomultiplier tube (photocathode, dynodes, anode), deuterium lamp, tungsten-halogen lamp, xenon lamp, hollow cathode lamp, holmium oxide filter, didymium filter, neutral-density filter.
explanation.why: A part that does not suit the wavelength silently ruins results: glass absorbs short-wavelength UV, a tungsten-halogen lamp is weak below 400 nm, and wavelength accuracy needs its own check, separate from photometric (absorbance) accuracy. Within the Beer’s law range, absorbance rises in proportion to path length, so path length is part of the calculation.
explanation.measure: Order: source → wavelength selector → cuvette → detector → readout. Deuterium = UV continuum (one review: about 160–400 nm); tungsten-halogen = visible; xenon = broad UV into visible; hollow cathode lamp = element-specific lines for atomic absorption. Glass absorbs UV-B and UV-C; quartz/fused silica transmits them. Standard path 10 mm; absorbance ∝ path length (Beer’s law range). PMT: dynode cascade, amplification of the order of a million-fold or more, gain set by dynode voltage. Holmium oxide glass: sharp certified bands (11 NIST bands, about 241–638 nm, including 360.8 nm), wavelength scale only.
explanation.differs: Deuterium (UV) vs tungsten-halogen (visible) vs hollow cathode (one element); glass vs quartz cuvettes; holmium oxide (sharp bands, wavelength) vs didymium (broad bands) vs neutral-density filters (absorbance scale).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the cuvette for a UV assay, name the lamp for UV or visible work, order the light-path parts, identify the PMT as the amplifying detector, or pick holmium oxide as the wavelength-accuracy check.

questions.stem: A protein assay is read at 280 nm. The signal reaching the detector is almost zero with the cuvette in place. Which cuvette should be used?

options.rationale: Correct. Quartz transmits short-wavelength UV that glass absorbs.
Incorrect. Glass absorbs UV-B and UV-C light, so cleaning does not help at 280 nm.
Incorrect. Plastic has a narrower usable wavelength range than glass or quartz.
Incorrect. A longer path does not fix the material problem; the glass still absorbs the UV.

questions.stem: In a UV-visible spectrophotometer, which lamp is the usual source for the visible region?

options.rationale: Correct. It covers the visible region but is weak below 400 nm.
Incorrect. Deuterium gives a continuum in the ultraviolet.
Incorrect. It emits the lines of one element and is used in atomic absorption.
Incorrect. Its line spectrum is used mainly for calibration, not as a continuous source.

questions.stem: A holmium oxide glass filter is scanned on a spectrophotometer during quality checks. What does this test?

options.rationale: Correct. Its sharp absorption bands have certified wavelength positions.
Incorrect. Holmium filters should not be used for the transmittance scale; neutral-density filters are used.
Incorrect. PMT gain depends on the dynode voltage; holmium certifies band positions.
Incorrect. Path length is a property of the cuvette, not of a wavelength standard.

claims.text: Light path order: source → wavelength selector (prism or grating) → cuvette → detector → readout.

Deuterium = UV continuum; tungsten-halogen = visible, weak below 400 nm; xenon = broad UV into visible; hollow cathode lamp = element-specific lines in atomic absorption; low-pressure Hg lines mainly for calibration.
Glass absorbs UV-B/UV-C while quartz transmits them; 280 nm needs quartz; standard path 10 mm; absorbance proportional to path length; plastic has the narrowest range.
PMT photocathode → dynode cascade → anode; amplification of the order of a million-fold or more; gain depends on interdynode voltage (100–200 V in one review); photodiodes as alternatives.
Holmium oxide sharp certified bands (including 360.8 nm) check wavelength only; neutral-density filters for transmittance; didymium bands too wide for wavelength checking.
Glass 350–2000 nm range and the 350 nm quartz cut-off; deuterium lamp ~100 V; ~90 V per dynode; didymium ~600 nm peak; interference-filter bandwidths.
claims.note: Not taught as facts in this lesson; no open source read gives these figures.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 4 Hit 21 lists didymium glass (~600 nm, broad peak) and holmium oxide (360 nm, sharp peak) as wavelength checks. Reule 1976 judged didymium bands too wide, temperature-dependent and of variable composition for wavelength checking; Allen 2007 lists 11 certified holmium bands (360.8 nm is one) and warns that holmium filters must not be used for the transmittance (absorbance) scale, which uses neutral-density filters. The lesson teaches holmium as the wavelength check and the didymium caveat (register flag rv-ch4-didymium-wavelength-check).

Ch. 4 Hit 6 gives ~90 V between dynodes and amplification up to ~10⁶. Michail 2024 gives 100–200 V between dynodes and an overall gain of the order of 10⁶, and Zheng 2020 “more than a million times”, so the gain figure is roughly consistent but 10⁶ is not a ceiling; figures depend on tube design and operating voltage. The lesson teaches the cascade, gain of about a million-fold or more and voltage-dependent gain, not 90 V (register flag rv-ch4-pmt-dynode-figures).

Ch. 4 Hit 5 and Trap 2 give 350 nm as the glass/quartz cut-off. The open sources read state that glass transmits UV-A (315–400 nm) but absorbs UV-B and UV-C, and that UV transmission differs between glasses; no source read gives 350 nm. The 280 nm trap answer (use quartz) stands. The lesson teaches the qualitative rule (register flag rv-ch4-glass-uv-cutoff).
